<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is a desktop application built on Electron that wraps the Microsoft Teams web client in a standalone shell for Linux (and other OSes).  
   - It is neither a traditional full-stack web app nor a microservice system; it’s a single-process Electron app with multiple renderer windows and modular features.

2. High-Level Architectural Components  
   a. Operating System  
      • Linux (with support for other OSes via the Electron layer)  
   b. Electron Runtime  
      • Main Process – orchestrates windows, modules, native integrations, packaging  
      • Renderer Processes – BrowserWindow instances that host web content or HTML UIs:  
        – Main Teams window (webview)  
        – Login window  
        – Stream selector window  
   c. Internal Modules (all loaded by the Main Process)  
      • appConfiguration – runtime settings loader  
      • config & logger – feature flags, logging configuration  
      • connectionManager – manages network events, offline/online state  
      • certificate – custom certificate handling for webview  
      • customBackground & customCSS – user-supplied UI tweaks  
      • spellCheckProvider – spellcheck dictionaries and API hooking  
      • intune – optional enterprise integration  
      • menus – application menu and tray menu management  
      • helpers – utility libraries  
   d. Build & Packaging  
      • scripts/afterpack.js and build/* manifest files generate AppImage, snap, deb, rpm, tar.gz  
   e. External Services  
      • Microsoft Teams web servers (HTTPS)  
      • OS native APIs (notifications, tray, file system)  
      • Extension points (firejail sandbox script, AppImageLauncher)

3. Interactions and Data Flow  
   - On launch, Main Process loads appConfiguration → config → logger → modules.  
   - Main Process creates the main BrowserWindow, preloading custom scripts (settings, theme, shortcuts, etc.).  
   - Renderer (webview) loads teams.microsoft.com → standard Teams UI.  
   - IPC channels connect Renderer ↔ Main for events (new meetings, notifications, spellcheck).  
   - User triggers in UI (e.g., change theme, custom CSS) → Renderer sends IPC to Main → Main applies settings dynamically.  
   - ConnectionManager monitors connectivity and informs Renderer via IPC.  
   - Menus and tray icons are controlled by Main and emit events into Renderer or other modules.  

4. Key Architectural Patterns & Principles  
   - Modular Main Process: each feature is a self-contained module under `app/`  
   - Clear separation between Main and Renderer (Electron’s multi-process model)  
   - IPC for cross-process communication  
   - Configuration-driven behavior (JSON + README docs in `app/config`)  
   - Plugin-style hooking: customCSS and customBackground load user assets at runtime  

5. Diagram Guidelines for an Electron Desktop App  
   - Draw a top-level “Electron Runtime” container with two lanes:  
     1. Main Process (left): list modules as sub-components (appConfiguration, config, certificate, connectionManager, menus, spellCheckProvider, customCSS, customBackground, intune, helpers)  
     2. Renderer Processes (right): three boxes – Main Teams Window, Login Window, Stream Selector Window. Show preload scripts feeding into each renderer.  
   - Show IPC arrows between Main Process modules and each Renderer box.  
   - Illustrate external connections: → Microsoft Teams Web Servers, → OS APIs (Notifications, Tray, FileSystem).  
   - Add build/packaging layer beneath Main Process pointing to build scripts and output packages (AppImage, deb, rpm, snap).  

6. Tailoring to This Project  
   - Emphasize the Electron dual-process model.  
   - Group feature modules under “Main Process” rather than as microservices.  
   - Distinguish between webview content (Teams UI) and native UIs (login.html, streamSelector.html).  
   - Highlight custom user-tweak modules (CSS, background, shortcuts).  
   - Include packaging targets to show deliverable formats.  

7. Diagram Styling Recommendations  
   - Label each component clearly (e.g., “ConnectionManager”, “SpellCheckProvider”).  
   - Use directional arrows to show:  
     • IPC requests/responses between Main ↔ Renderer  
     • HTTP(S) requests to Teams servers  
     • Calls to OS native APIs  
   - Color Coding:  
     • Blue boxes for Main Process modules  
     • Green boxes for Renderer windows  
     • Orange arrows for network traffic  
     • Gray boxes/arrows for build/packaging  
   - Shapes:  
     • Rectangle for processes/modules  
     • Cylinders for external services/datastores  
     • Dashed lines for optional features (e.g., Intune, firejail integration)  

By following this structure and level of detail, your system design diagram will faithfully reflect the Teams-for-Linux application architecture, clearly depicting how Electron’s Main and Renderer processes collaborate with modular features and external services.  
</explanation>
